extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, press-freedom advocates, researchers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic, chronological account of incidents, legal rulings, datasets, and policy responses documenting attacks on journalists and constraints on newsgathering in the United States from the 1999 WTO protests through mid-2020s events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters Without Borders World Press Freedom Index scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Press Freedom Index score bands and classifications used to evaluate national press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: 85–100 points; Satisfactory: 70–85 points; Problematic: 55–70 points; Difficult: 40–55 points; Very serious: <40 points. (Article cites U.S. rankings over time: e.g., 49th in 2015 and 57th in 2025.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable-cause requirement for arresting journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have applied the legal standard that police must have probable cause of a crime before arresting, dispersing, or using force against journalists and legal observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal jury/federal-court rulings found police lacked probable cause in major sweeps (e.g., WTO week) and courts barred arrests/force absent probable cause (e.g., Portland rulings). These findings produced damages, settlements, and injunctions restricting police tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions from security zones and rolling dispersal orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Access restrictions and rolling dispersal orders can constrain where reporters can safely stand to observe and document events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate rulings upheld portions of downtown security zones while noting how such measures limited reporters' ability to observe; these constraints are cited as impeding newsgathering and creating legal/operational tension between security measures and press access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of militarized policing and less-lethal weapons that impede newsgathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavily militarized policing tactics (large interagency deployments, less-lethal munitions, concussion/flash-bang devices, rubber bullets, tear gas, pepper spray) used during protests that exposed and harmed journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the 'Miami model' at the 2003 FTAA meetings and widespread use of chemical agents and projectiles (e.g., Ferguson, George Floyd protests). Press-freedom groups documented physical injuries, equipment damage, and chilling effects; subsequent reviews criticized such tactics and cited them in litigation and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective credentialing and embedded-reporter practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices of selective credentialing — embedding some reporters with police/security units while sidelining non-embedded journalists — affect who can safely and lawfully cover events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Miami model' and other operations used selective credentialing; civil-liberties groups condemned treating non-embedded journalists as ordinary demonstrators. Embedding may grant closer access but can marginalize independent/alternative media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure and search of equipment and storage media (including border searches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Searches, seizures, and confiscations of cameras, phones, storage media, and other equipment that interfere with reporting and raise source-confidentiality concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents cited include equipment seized during mass arrests, devices seized at borders (e.g., Standing Rock / Canada–U.S. border detention), and cameras damaged during dispersals. Reporters Without Borders, ACLU, and HRW documented how such practices chilled newsgathering and source communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass detention/sweep arrest tactics that include journalists and observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Kettling and mass 'sweep' arrest operations that net journalists, legal observers, and bystanders alongside protesters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: WTO week downtown sweep, RNC mass arrests, kettling incidents in St. Paul and D.C. Such tactics led to litigation, findings of lack of probable cause, damages, and policy reforms; they are identified as practices that chill protest coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force against clearly identified journalists is unlawful/problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Documented instances where journalists were struck, pepper-sprayed, or otherwise subjected to force despite identifying themselves as press are treated as violations of press freedom and have been the subject of litigation and oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases (e.g., Occupy, Ferguson, George Floyd protests, RNC coverage) recorded assaults on credentialed reporters. Courts and oversight bodies in some jurisdictions curtailed use of force against media and mandated training following such incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credentialing (press passes) as a practical protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of an official press pass (e.g., NYPD press pass) is described as reducing arrest risk, but access to such credentials may be limited or require meeting difficult standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials advised that an NYPD press pass would reduce arrest risk during Occupy, yet new passes were temporarily unavailable and required proof of crossing police lines—difficult without credentials—illustrating practical barriers to obtaining protective credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Freedom Tracker incident categories and quantitative measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorization and counting of incidents affecting journalists (arrests, equipment destruction/seizure, physical attacks, tear gassings, pepper sprayings, rubber-bullet incidents) as a way to measure scale and severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Press Freedom Tracker recorded detailed incident counts (example: between May 28 and June 1 it reported 49 arrests, 42 instances of destruction of equipment, 69 physical attacks, 43 tear gassings, 24 pepper sprayings, and 77 rubber-bullet incidents), providing empirical evidence used by outlets and advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy reforms following litigation (training, limits on pepper spray, dispersal-order practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlements and oversight sometimes require police/agencies to adopt reforms — e.g., training, limits on use of pepper spray, and clearer dispersal-order practices — to protect journalists and observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: District of Columbia agreed to pay $1.6 million and adopt reforms including training, limits on pepper spray, and clearer dispersal-order practices after litigation arising from mass arrests that affected press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate charging and prosecution standards for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutorial decisions to bring riot or related charges against journalists are scrutinized; lack of probable cause or inappropriate charging has led to dismissals and criticism from press-freedom groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Charges sought or brought against reporters at Standing Rock and during the 2017 inauguration were later dismissed or dropped for lack of probable cause; press advocates flagged such prosecutions as deterring coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveillance, secrecy, and intelligence-sharing practices that chill reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-9/11 expansions of secrecy and surveillance (USA PATRIOT Act, FISA, fusion centers), and institutional practices (border searches of electronic devices) are described as deterring sources and impeding newsgathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human Rights Watch/ACLU studies and press-freedom monitors linked increased surveillance and intelligence-sharing to measurable declines in press freedom and reduced willingness of sources to communicate with reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police photographing journalists and credentials as an intimidation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of photographing journalists and their credentials by police is criticized as an intimidating tactic and a violation of press protection norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Brooklyn Center, credential-photography by police was publicized and criticized by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and the ACLU; following criticism, some agencies said they would stop photographing journalists.
